lessons.title: Bacteria, viruses and why the difference matters

scenes.text: Rohan has a sore throat, runny nose and mild fever for two days.
He asks for 'a strong antibiotic' to recover before his presentation.
The doctor explains why that won't help — and might harm.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Two different worlds
steps.body: **Bacteria** are living single cells with their own cell wall, ribosomes and metabolism. **Viruses** are genetic material in a protein coat that must hijack our cells to multiply — they have **no cell wall and no bacterial ribosomes**, so antibiotics have nothing to hit.

steps.title: Usually viral
steps.body: Most colds, flu, most sore throats, most acute bronchitis, dengue, chikungunya and COVID-19 are viral. Antibiotics don't shorten them. Some viruses have specific **antivirals** (e.g. oseltamivir for influenza, HIV antiretrovirals) — different medicines.

steps.title: Typically bacterial
steps.body: Strep throat (some), urinary tract infections, many pneumonias, typhoid, tuberculosis, cellulitis, some ear and sinus infections — a doctor decides using examination and sometimes tests (culture, blood counts, CRP).

activity.prompt: Usually caused by viruses or bacteria?

quiz.q: Antibiotics don't work on viruses because viruses…
options: Lack bacterial targets like cell walls and bacterial ribosomes

quiz.q: Most colds should be treated with…

lessons.title: Match the antibiotic to its target

scenes.text: Dr Fernandes draws a bacterium on the board with five arrows pointing to its weak spots.
Each arrow is an antibiotic class.

steps.title: Cell wall
steps.body: **Beta-lactams** — penicillins (amoxicillin), cephalosporins (cefixime, ceftriaxone), carbapenems (meropenem) — block **penicillin-binding proteins** that build peptidoglycan; the wall weakens and the bacterium bursts. **Vancomycin** blocks wall building differently.

steps.title: Protein synthesis (ribosome)
steps.body: Bacterial ribosomes are **70S** (50S + 30S); ours are 80S. **Macrolides** (azithromycin) and **linezolid** hit 50S; **tetracyclines** (doxycycline) and **aminoglycosides** (gentamicin) hit 30S.

steps.title: DNA and folate
steps.body: **Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) block **DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV**. **Sulfonamides + trimethoprim** block folate synthesis. **Rifampicin** blocks bacterial RNA polymerase (key in TB).

steps.title: Cidal vs static; spectrum
steps.body: **Bactericidal** drugs kill; **bacteriostatic** stop growth so immunity can finish the job. **Broad-spectrum** drugs hit many species (more gut-flora damage and resistance pressure); **narrow-spectrum** target fewer. Doctors aim for the narrowest effective drug.

activity.prompt: Match the class to its target.

quiz.q: Why prefer narrow spectrum when possible?
options: Less collateral damage and resistance pressure

lessons.title: Lab: Side effects and allergy

scenes.text: After a few days of amoxicillin, a young adult develops an itchy, raised rash.
Allergy? Or something else? It matters for the rest of his life.

steps.title: Allergy
steps.body: Penicillin allergy ranges from rashes to **anaphylaxis** (112, adrenaline). Severe skin reactions (**Stevens–Johnson syndrome/TEN**: blistering, peeling skin, mouth sores, fever) are emergencies. Record genuine allergies; many 'penicillin allergy' labels turn out to be wrong on specialist testing, so a doctor should evaluate.

steps.title: Common side effects
steps.body: Diarrhoea and nausea (gut flora disruption), thrush (yeast overgrowth), and **C. difficile** colitis (severe watery diarrhoea, cramps — see a doctor).

steps.title: Class-specific cautions
steps.body:
- **Fluoroquinolones:** tendon rupture, nerve damage, aortic aneurysm concerns — regulators restrict use for minor infections
- **Tetracyclines:** tooth staining in young children, sun sensitivity; take upright with water
- **Aminoglycosides:** kidney and hearing damage (monitored)
- **Macrolides:** QT prolongation, interactions
- **Metronidazole:** labels warn against alcohol

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Demanding antibiotics for colds and flu
- Assuming a rash means lifelong penicillin allergy without evaluation
- Using fluoroquinolones for minor infections
- Ignoring severe diarrhoea after antibiotics

activity.prompt: Emergency (112/urgent) or discuss with doctor soon?

steps.title: Decision logic
steps.body: Likely bacterial? Serious? Evidence from exam/tests? Narrowest effective drug, right duration, allergy check, review with culture results. When unsure and the patient is well, **watchful waiting** with clear return advice is often right.

steps.title: Common mistakes

courses.title: Antimicrobial resistance and using antibiotics right
courses.summary: How bacteria become resistant (mutation, gene transfer, selection), superbugs and India's AMR challenge, the Red Line campaign and Schedule H1, completing courses as prescribed, and what everyone can do.
outcomes: Learners can explain how resistance evolves and spreads
Learners can describe India's Red Line and Schedule H1 measures
Learners can explain why to follow prescribed courses and never share antibiotics
Learners can list One Health drivers of AMR

lessons.title: How resistance evolves

scenes.text: In an ICU, a patient's infection does not respond to carbapenems — once a 'last resort'.
The bacterium carries a gene that destroys the drug.
How did it get here?

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Natural selection in fast-forward
steps.body: Bacteria divide in as little as 20 minutes. Random **mutations** occasionally make one resistant. When an antibiotic kills the susceptible ones, the resistant survivors multiply — **selection**. Every unnecessary course adds selection pressure.

steps.title: Sharing genes
steps.body: Bacteria pass resistance genes on **plasmids** by **conjugation**, take up DNA (**transformation**) or get it via viruses (**transduction**). So resistance can jump between species. Example mechanisms: enzymes like **beta-lactamases** (e.g. ESBLs, NDM-1 carbapenemase), efflux pumps, altered targets, reduced entry.

steps.title: Scale
steps.body: A major global analysis (GRAM, Lancet 2022) estimated bacterial AMR was directly responsible for about **1.27 million deaths in 2019** and associated with about 4.95 million. India has among the world's highest burdens of resistant infections.

activity.prompt: Order how resistance spreads in a population of bacteria.
items: A random mutation makes one bacterium resistant
An antibiotic is taken unnecessarily
Susceptible bacteria die
Resistant survivors multiply
Resistance gene moves to other bacteria on a plasmid
Resistant infection spreads to other people

quiz.q: Plasmid gene transfer between bacteria by contact is…
Bacterial AMR directly caused about how many deaths in 2019 (GRAM)?

lessons.title: India's rules — Red Line and Schedule H1

scenes.text: Meena notices a vertical red line on her antibiotic strip.
She has never noticed it before. What does it mean?

steps.title: Red Line campaign (2016)
steps.body: India's health ministry promoted a **vertical red line** on packs of prescription-only antibiotics and other key medicines: it means **'do not use without a doctor's prescription'**.

steps.title: Schedule H1 (2014)
steps.body: Many third/fourth-generation antibiotics, anti-TB drugs and some habit-forming drugs are in **Schedule H1** of the Drugs Rules. Pharmacies must sell them only on prescription and maintain a register (prescriber, patient, drug, quantity).

steps.title: National Action Plan
steps.body: India's **National Action Plan on AMR (2017)** follows a **One Health** approach: human health, animals, agriculture and environment. Colistin as an animal growth promoter was banned in 2019.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping leftovers 'for next time'
- Sharing antibiotics with family
- Buying Red Line medicines without prescription
- Stopping or extending a course without asking the doctor

statements.s: A red vertical line on a strip means 'prescription only'.
Schedule H1 drugs can be sold freely without records.
One Health links human, animal and environmental health.
India banned colistin as an animal growth promoter in 2019.

quiz.q: The Red Line on a pack means…
options: Don't use without a doctor's prescription

lessons.title: Lab: Courses, leftovers and sharing

scenes.text: Amit felt better on day 3 of his prescribed antibiotic and stopped, keeping the rest 'for next time'.
Months later his wife has a cough and he offers her the leftovers.

steps.title: Follow the prescribed course
steps.body: Take the antibiotic exactly as prescribed — dose, timing and duration. Modern evidence shows **shorter courses** work for many infections, and doctors increasingly prescribe them; so the right duration is the one your doctor sets, not 'until I feel better' nor 'longer to be safe'. Ask your doctor before stopping early. For some infections (e.g. **TB**), completing long regimens is critical to cure and to prevent drug-resistant TB.

steps.title: Never
steps.body:
- Self-start leftover antibiotics
- Share antibiotics
- Pressure doctors for antibiotics for colds
- Buy 'Red Line' antibiotics without prescription

steps.title: Prevent infections
steps.body: Hand washing, safe water, vaccination, safe food handling and safe sex reduce the need for antibiotics in the first place.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Keeping leftovers 'for next time'
- Sharing antibiotics with family
- Buying Red Line medicines without prescription
- Stopping or extending a course without asking the doctor

steps.body: Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before starting, stopping or combining medicines, and whenever symptoms are severe, unusual or not improving. In an emergency call **112**. For mental-health support call Tele-MANAS **14416**; for a child in danger call **1098**.

courses.title: Vaccines and immunity
courses.summary: Innate and adaptive immunity, memory cells, vaccine types (live attenuated, inactivated, subunit/toxoid, mRNA, viral vector), herd immunity, side effects vs myths, and the history of eradication.
outcomes: Learners can explain how vaccines create immune memory
Learners can classify vaccine types

lessons.title: How immunity remembers

story.title: The second chickenpox that never came

scenes.text: Zoya had chickenpox at age 6. Her brother caught it from her friend years later — she didn't.
Her immune system remembered.
Vaccines teach that memory without the disease.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Two layers
steps.body: **Innate immunity**: fast, non-specific (skin, mucus, neutrophils, macrophages, fever, inflammation). **Adaptive immunity**: slower, specific — **B cells** make **antibodies**, **T cells** (helper CD4, killer CD8) coordinate and kill infected cells.

steps.title: Memory
steps.body: After the first encounter (**primary response**, days to weeks), long-lived **memory B and T cells** remain. On re-exposure the **secondary response** is faster, stronger and more specific — often stopping illness before symptoms.

steps.title: Active vs passive
steps.body: **Active immunity**: your body makes it (infection or vaccine) — lasting. **Passive**: ready-made antibodies (mother's antibodies through placenta/breast milk, anti-rabies immunoglobulin, antivenom) — immediate but temporary.

activity.prompt: Match the immune player to its job.

quiz.q: Maternal antibodies to the baby are…

lessons.title: Lab: Types of vaccines

scenes.text: A health centre fridge holds BCG, OPV, IPV, pentavalent, rotavirus and MR vaccines.
They are made in very different ways.

steps.title: Main types
steps.body:
- **Live attenuated:** weakened germ (BCG, MR/MMR, oral polio OPV, rotavirus, yellow fever, varicella) — strong immunity; generally avoided in pregnancy and severe immunosuppression
- **Inactivated:** killed germ (IPV, hepatitis A, rabies vaccines)
- **Subunit/recombinant:** pieces of the germ (hepatitis B, HPV)
- **Toxoid:** inactivated toxin (tetanus, diphtheria)
- **Conjugate:** sugar coat linked to protein (Hib, pneumococcal PCV) — works in infants
- **mRNA** and **viral vector** (several COVID-19 vaccines)

steps.title: Cold chain
steps.body: Most vaccines need **2–8 °C** storage; some are damaged by freezing, others by heat. India's **eVIN** system tracks vaccine stock and temperatures digitally.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing debunked autism claims
- Delaying vaccines 'until the child is stronger'
- Breaking the cold chain at home or in transport
- Thinking rare diseases no longer need vaccines

activity.prompt: Classify each vaccine.

quiz.q: Live vaccines are generally avoided in…

lessons.title: Lab: Herd immunity numbers

scenes.text: A town's measles vaccine coverage slipped to 80%.
An outbreak starts. Why wasn't 80% enough?

steps.title: R0 and the threshold
steps.body:
**R0** = average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. The herd immunity threshold is approximately **1 − 1/R0**.

Measles R0 is about 12–18 → threshold about 92–95%. Polio (R0 ~5–7) → ~80–86%.

steps.title: Who herd immunity protects
steps.body: Newborns too young for vaccines, people on chemotherapy, and those who can't be vaccinated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing debunked autism claims
- Delaying vaccines 'until the child is stronger'
- Breaking the cold chain at home or in transport
- Thinking rare diseases no longer need vaccines

activity.prompt: A disease has R0 = 5. Using 1 − 1/R0, what percentage of the population must be immune for herd immunity?

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — answer the vaccine myths

scenes.text: Your aunt forwards: 'Vaccines cause autism and overload babies' immunity.'
Reply with calm, evidence-based answers.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body:
- The 1998 paper claiming MMR causes autism was **retracted** (2010) and its author struck off; large studies of millions of children found no link.
- Babies' immune systems handle countless antigens daily; schedules are designed and tested.
- Common side effects: sore arm, mild fever, fussiness for a day or two. Serious reactions are rare; staff are trained to manage anaphylaxis.
- **AEFI** (adverse events following immunisation) are monitored by national surveillance.

steps.title: What vaccines achieved
steps.body: Smallpox eradicated (declared 1980). India removed from polio-endemic list 2012 and WHO South-East Asia Region certified polio-free in March 2014. India validated for maternal and neonatal tetanus elimination in 2015.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing debunked autism claims
- Delaying vaccines 'until the child is stronger'
- Breaking the cold chain at home or in transport
- Thinking rare diseases no longer need vaccines

a.text: Your aunt posts: 'Vaccines cause autism — I'm skipping MR for my grandson.' How do you reply first?

choices.label: Privately, kindly: ask what worried her and share that the autism study was retracted and huge studies found no link
Publicly mock her in the family group

b.text: She asks: 'But isn't natural measles better for immunity?'

choices.label: Explain measles can cause pneumonia, brain swelling and death; the vaccine gives protection without that risk
Say 'just trust me'
choices.feedback: Facts persuade better than authority alone.

choices.label: Offer to go with her to talk to the ANM or paediatrician and check the card for due doses
Give up

bad.text: She leaves the group angry and avoids the topic. Try a private, respectful approach.

end1.text: The child gets MR at the next session. Calm evidence and support worked.

end2.text: Measles outbreaks happen when coverage drops. Keep the conversation open.

lessons.title: From EPI to UIP to Indradhanush

scenes.text: ASHA worker Lata visits a new mother in her village with an immunisation card.
She explains which vaccines are free and when they are due.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: History
steps.body: India began the **Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)** in **1978**. It became the **Universal Immunization Programme (UIP)** in **1985**, one of the largest public-health programmes in the world, reaching tens of millions of newborns and pregnant women every year with vaccines that are **free** at government facilities and outreach sessions.

steps.title: Mission Indradhanush
steps.body: Launched in **December 2014** to reach children and pregnant women who were unvaccinated or partially vaccinated, focusing on high-priority districts and urban slums; **Intensified Mission Indradhanush** followed in 2017. New vaccines added over the years include rotavirus, pneumococcal conjugate (PCV), IPV and measles-rubella (MR).

steps.title: Who delivers it
steps.body: **ANMs** (auxiliary nurse midwives) vaccinate at health centres and village session sites; **ASHA** workers mobilise families; **Anganwadi** workers help track children. Cold-chain points and the eVIN system keep vaccines potent.

lessons.title: What the UIP protects against

scenes.text: The card lists BCG, OPV, Hep B, Pentavalent, Rotavirus, PCV, IPV, MR, JE, DPT boosters and Td.

steps.title: Key vaccines
steps.body:
- **BCG** — severe childhood TB (TB meningitis)
- **OPV + IPV** — polio
- **Hepatitis B** (birth dose) — hepatitis B
- **Pentavalent** — diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), tetanus, hepatitis B, Hib
- **Rotavirus** — severe diarrhoea
- **PCV** — pneumococcal pneumonia
- **MR** — measles and rubella
- **JE** — Japanese encephalitis (in endemic districts)
- **DPT boosters, Td** — diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis
- **Td for pregnant women** — protects mother and newborn from tetanus
The exact schedule is set by the programme; follow the card and your health worker.

steps.title: Missed a dose?
steps.body: Don't restart the series. Visit the health centre or session site; the worker will give catch-up doses per the schedule.

- Not carrying the immunisation card
- Leaving before the 30-minute observation
- Not reporting serious reactions (AEFI)

lessons.title: The silent killer and the numbers

scenes.text: At a free office health camp, Suresh, 42, feels perfectly fine.
His BP reads 162/98 mmHg on two readings.
No symptoms — but real risk to his heart, brain and kidneys.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: The numbers
steps.body: **Systolic** (pressure when the heart beats) / **diastolic** (between beats), in mmHg. Hypertension is commonly diagnosed at **≥140/90 mmHg** on repeated clinic readings (some guidelines use lower thresholds). Diagnosis needs several readings, ideally with home or ambulatory monitoring.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Uncontrolled hypertension damages arteries and is a leading cause of **stroke, heart attack, heart failure, kidney disease** and vision loss. Often there are no symptoms until damage occurs. India's NCD programmes screen adults over 30.

steps.title: Lifestyle is treatment too
steps.body: Less salt, more vegetables/fruit, weight loss, regular activity, limiting alcohol, not smoking and good sleep can lower BP meaningfully — alongside medicines when needed.

bands.text: Normal range for most adults (with diastolic under 80).
Hypertension range on repeated readings — see a doctor.
Higher hypertension — doctor soon; treatment likely.
Very high (≥180) — seek prompt medical care; with chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, confusion or vision loss call 112.

quiz.q: Hypertension is called a silent killer because…

lessons.title: Lab: Decode the drug classes

scenes.text: Suresh's father takes telmisartan, amlodipine and chlorthalidone. His uncle takes enalapril and metoprolol.
The endings of the names tell you the class.

steps.title: ACE inhibitors (-pril)
steps.body: Enalapril, ramipril, lisinopril block **angiotensin-converting enzyme**, so less angiotensin II (a vessel-tightener and salt-retainer). Side effects: **dry cough** (from bradykinin build-up), high potassium, rare **angioedema** (face/tongue swelling — emergency). Not in pregnancy.

steps.title: ARBs (-sartan)
steps.body: Telmisartan, losartan, olmesartan block the angiotensin II **AT1 receptor**. Similar benefits, much less cough. Also not in pregnancy; monitor kidney function and potassium.

steps.title: Calcium channel blockers
steps.body: **Amlodipine** (dihydropyridine) relaxes artery muscle by blocking L-type calcium channels. Side effects: **ankle swelling**, flushing, headache. Verapamil/diltiazem also slow the heart.

steps.title: Diuretics and beta blockers
steps.body: **Thiazide-type** (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, indapamide) increase salt and water loss; can lower sodium/potassium, raise sugar/uric acid. **Beta blockers (-olol)** (metoprolol, atenolol, bisoprolol) slow the heart; useful after heart attack or in heart failure; can cause tiredness, cold hands, and mask low-sugar symptoms; caution in asthma.

lessons.title: Lab: Home BP measurement done right

scenes.text: Suresh buys a home BP machine and measures right after climbing stairs with coffee in hand.
His readings jump everywhere. Technique matters.

steps.title: Technique
steps.body: Validated upper-arm automatic device, correct cuff size, sit quietly for 5 minutes, back supported, feet flat, arm at heart level, no caffeine/exercise/smoking for 30 minutes, empty bladder, don't talk. Take 2 readings a minute apart, morning and evening, for several days; record them.

steps.title: White-coat and masked hypertension
steps.body: Some people read high only in clinic (**white-coat**); others read normal in clinic but high at home (**masked**). Home monitoring helps doctors decide.

steps.title: Don't self-adjust
steps.body: Do not stop or change BP medicines based on a few readings. Share your log with your doctor. Dizziness on standing may mean the dose needs review.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping tablets once readings are normal
- Measuring BP right after tea, stairs or a cigarette
- Silently stopping a drug because of a side effect instead of telling the doctor
- Using potassium salt substitutes on ACE inhibitors/ARBs without advice

lessons.title: Diabetes basics and HbA1c

scenes.text: Lakshmi, 48, is told she has 'thoda sugar'. Her HbA1c is 8.2%.
What does that number mean, and why does it matter?

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Insulin and glucose
steps.body: **Insulin** from pancreatic **beta cells** lets glucose enter muscle, fat and liver cells. **Type 1 diabetes**: autoimmune destruction of beta cells → little/no insulin → insulin is essential from diagnosis. **Type 2**: insulin resistance plus gradually failing insulin secretion; linked to genetics, abdominal weight, inactivity. India has one of the world's largest diabetes populations.

steps.title: HbA1c
steps.body: Glucose attaches to haemoglobin; **HbA1c** reflects average glucose over about **2–3 months**. Diabetes is diagnosed at **≥6.5%**; 5.7–6.4% is commonly called prediabetes. Many adults aim for around 7% or below, individualised by the doctor.

steps.title: Why control matters
steps.body: High glucose damages small vessels (eyes, kidneys, nerves) and large vessels (heart attack, stroke, foot problems). Good control, BP and cholesterol management and not smoking reduce complications.

statements.s: Type 1 diabetes needs insulin from diagnosis.
HbA1c reflects about the last 2–3 months of glucose.
HbA1c of 6.5% or higher can diagnose diabetes.
Type 2 diabetes is only caused by eating sugar.

lessons.title: Lab: Metformin — mechanism and cautions

scenes.text: Lakshmi starts metformin and gets loose stools in the first week.
She wonders whether to quit.

steps.title: How it works
steps.body: **Metformin** (a biguanide) mainly **reduces glucose production by the liver** (gluconeogenesis) and improves insulin sensitivity; it acts partly via cellular energy pathways (AMPK) and the gut. It does **not** stimulate insulin release, so alone it rarely causes low sugar. Often first-line for type 2, weight-neutral or modest weight loss.

steps.title: Side effects
steps.body:
- **GI upset** (nausea, diarrhoea, metallic taste) — often settles; taking with meals and slow dose increases (doctor-guided) or extended-release forms help
- **Vitamin B12 deficiency** with long-term use — periodic checks
- **Lactic acidosis** — rare but serious; risk with severe kidney impairment, severe dehydration, shock, heavy alcohol

steps.title: When doctors pause it
steps.body: Severe kidney impairment, serious illness with dehydration ('sick days' — vomiting/diarrhoea), around some iodinated contrast scans and major surgery — per the doctor's instruction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping meals while on sulfonylureas
- Quitting metformin in week one for mild stomach upset without talking to the doctor
- Giving food or drink to an unconscious person with low sugar
- Not checking B12 after years of metformin

activity.prompt: Metformin: true facts vs myths.

items.text: It strongly forces the pancreas to release insulin

Doctors may pause it in severe dehydration

lessons.title: Lab: Low sugar (hypoglycaemia) — the 15–15 rule

scenes.text: Mr Bose, on glimepiride, skipped lunch for a meeting.
At 3 pm he is sweaty, shaky, confused and irritable.

steps.title: Who is at risk
steps.body: **Sulfonylureas** (glimepiride, gliclazide, glibenclamide) stimulate insulin release regardless of glucose → can cause **hypoglycaemia**, especially with missed meals, exercise, alcohol, kidney disease, older age. Insulin also causes it.

steps.title: Symptoms
steps.body: Shaking, sweating, fast heartbeat, hunger, anxiety → then confusion, slurred speech, odd behaviour (mistaken for drunkenness), seizures, unconsciousness. Usually glucose **below 70 mg/dL**.

steps.title: The 15–15 rule (if awake and able to swallow)
steps.body: Give **15 g fast-acting sugar** (e.g. glucose tablets, 3 teaspoons sugar in water, ~150 mL regular juice or non-diet soft drink). Recheck in **15 minutes**; repeat if still low. Then eat a snack/meal with starch. **Never give food or drink to someone unconscious** — recovery position and **call 112** (glucagon if available and trained).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping meals while on sulfonylureas
- Quitting metformin in week one for mild stomach upset without talking to the doctor
- Giving food or drink to an unconscious person with low sugar
- Not checking B12 after years of metformin

activity.prompt: Order the response to Mr Bose (awake, able to swallow).
items: Recognise symptoms and check glucose if possible
Give 15 g fast-acting sugar
Wait 15 minutes and recheck
Repeat sugar if still below 70 mg/dL
Give a starchy snack or meal once recovered
Inform his doctor about the episode

options: Nothing by mouth; recovery position; call 112

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — newer classes and sick-day rules

scenes.text: A year later, Lakshmi's doctor adds a new tablet.

steps.title: Newer classes
steps.body:
- **DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin):** sitagliptin, vildagliptin, teneligliptin — boost incretin hormones; low hypoglycaemia risk alone
- **SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin):** dapagliflozin, empagliflozin — make kidneys excrete glucose in urine; benefits for heart failure and kidney disease in many patients; risks: genital yeast infections, dehydration, rare **euglycaemic ketoacidosis**
- **GLP-1 receptor agonists:** injectable (and an oral form) — weight loss; GI side effects
- **Pioglitazone:** insulin sensitiser; fluid retention, weight gain

steps.title: Sick-day thinking
steps.body: When vomiting, unable to eat or dehydrated, doctors often advise temporarily pausing metformin, SGLT2 inhibitors and some BP drugs — **only per your own written sick-day plan from your doctor**. Check sugar more often; seek care for persistent vomiting, drowsiness or rapid breathing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Skipping meals while on sulfonylureas
- Quitting metformin in week one for mild stomach upset without talking to the doctor
- Giving food or drink to an unconscious person with low sugar
- Not checking B12 after years of metformin

lessons.title: Insulin types and profiles

scenes.text: Arjun, 19, was just diagnosed with type 1 diabetes and handed two insulin pens.
One for meals, one 'background'. Why two?

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Rapid-acting** (lispro, aspart, glulisine): start ~10–20 min, for meals
- **Short-acting/regular** (human soluble insulin): start ~30 min, taken earlier before meals
- **Intermediate** (NPH/isophane): cloudy, ~12–18 h
- **Long-acting** (glargine, detemir, degludec): basal, ~24 h or longer, fairly flat
- **Premixed** (e.g. 30/70): mix of short/rapid and intermediate

steps.title: Basal–bolus
steps.body: The body normally releases a steady **basal** insulin plus **bolus** spikes at meals. In type 1, regimens mimic this. Doses are set and adjusted by the diabetes team based on glucose logs, meals, activity — never copied from someone else.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Injecting in the same spot every time
- Leaving insulin in a hot car or freezing it
- Skipping basal insulin during illness (type 1)
- Sharing pens

lessons.title: Lab: Injection technique and site rotation

scenes.text: Arjun's sugars are erratic. The educator finds a rubbery lump on his belly where he always injects.
Lipohypertrophy — fixed by rotating sites.

steps.title: Pen technique
steps.body: Wash hands, check insulin type and expiry, attach a **new needle**, prime (air shot) as the pen instructs, select dose, inject into **subcutaneous fat** (abdomen, thighs, buttocks, upper arms), hold for ~10 seconds, remove and safely dispose of the needle.

steps.title: Rotate
steps.body: Repeated injections in one spot cause **lipohypertrophy** (lumps) where insulin absorbs unpredictably → highs and lows. Rotate within and between areas; avoid lumps, scars and bruises. Never share pens, even with a new needle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Injecting in the same spot every time
- Leaving insulin in a hot car or freezing it
- Skipping basal insulin during illness (type 1)
- Sharing pens

steps.title: Storage rules
steps.body: **Unopened**: refrigerator, **2–8 °C**, not in the freezer or touching the cooling element. **In-use** pen/vial: usually at room temperature (below about 25–30 °C per the product leaflet) for a limited number of weeks stated on the label. **Never freeze**; discard if frozen, clumped, or (for clear insulins) cloudy.

steps.title: Travel
steps.body: Carry insulin in hand luggage (never checked-in baggage — the hold can freeze), use an insulated pouch or evaporative cooling wallet in heat, carry a doctor's letter, extra supplies, glucose tablets and a glucometer. Plan time-zone changes with your team.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Skipping basal insulin during illness (type 1)
- Sharing pens

courses.title: Cholesterol medicines: statins and beyond
courses.summary: LDL, HDL and triglycerides, how statins work and lower heart-attack risk, muscle and liver side effects (and the 'nocebo' effect), interactions, and other options.

lessons.title: Reading a lipid profile

scenes.text: Deepak, 45, gets a lipid report: LDL 168, HDL 34, triglycerides 240 mg/dL.
Which matters most?

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: The parts
steps.body:
- **LDL** ('bad'): carries cholesterol into artery walls → atherosclerosis. Main treatment target.
- **HDL**: helps remove cholesterol; low HDL is a risk marker
- **Triglycerides**: raised with excess calories, alcohol, uncontrolled diabetes; very high levels risk pancreatitis
- **Non-HDL** = total − HDL

steps.title: Targets are personal
steps.body: LDL targets depend on overall risk: people with previous heart attack, diabetes with organ damage, or familial hypercholesterolaemia have much lower targets. Doctors use risk calculators and history.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping a statin because of mild aches without discussion
- Ignoring dark urine with severe muscle pain
- Thinking cholesterol is the only heart risk
- Taking statins while planning pregnancy without telling the doctor

activity.prompt: Total cholesterol is 230 mg/dL and HDL is 40 mg/dL. What is non-HDL cholesterol?

lessons.title: Lab: How statins work and who benefits

scenes.text: After Deepak's father's heart attack, he is prescribed atorvastatin.
The doctor draws the liver making cholesterol.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Statins (atorvastatin, rosuvastatin, simvastatin…) inhibit **HMG-CoA reductase**, the rate-limiting enzyme of cholesterol synthesis in the liver. The liver responds by making more **LDL receptors**, pulling LDL out of blood. They also stabilise plaques.

steps.title: Benefit
steps.body: Large trials show statins reduce heart attacks and strokes, with benefit proportional to LDL lowering and to baseline risk. Biggest gains: people with existing cardiovascular disease, diabetes, very high LDL.

steps.title: Not in pregnancy
steps.body: Statins are generally avoided in pregnancy and breastfeeding; tell your doctor if planning pregnancy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping a statin because of mild aches without discussion
- Ignoring dark urine with severe muscle pain
- Thinking cholesterol is the only heart risk
- Taking statins while planning pregnancy without telling the doctor

activity.prompt: Order how a statin lowers LDL.
items: Statin blocks HMG-CoA reductase in liver cells
Liver cells make less cholesterol
Cells sense low cholesterol
They make more LDL receptors
Receptors pull LDL from the blood
Blood LDL falls and heart-attack risk drops

lessons.title: Lab: Side effects, interactions and alternatives

scenes.text: Two months on a statin, Deepak's legs ache after gym.
Statin? Or his new workout?

steps.title: Muscle
steps.body: Muscle aches are commonly reported, though blinded trials show most aches occur similarly on placebo (**nocebo** effect). Rarely, true myopathy or **rhabdomyolysis** (severe muscle pain/weakness, dark cola-coloured urine) — urgent care. Doctors may check CK and adjust.

steps.title: Other cautions
steps.body: Liver enzyme rises (usually mild), small increase in diabetes risk (benefit usually outweighs). **Interactions**: some macrolides (clarithromycin), azole antifungals, some HIV drugs, gemfibrozil; **grapefruit** with simvastatin/atorvastatin.

steps.title: Alternatives/add-ons
steps.body: **Ezetimibe** (reduces gut absorption), **PCSK9 inhibitors** (injections, large LDL reductions), bempedoic acid, and lifestyle (fibre, less saturated/trans fat, activity, weight).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping a statin because of mild aches without discussion
- Ignoring dark urine with severe muscle pain
- Thinking cholesterol is the only heart risk
- Taking statins while planning pregnancy without telling the doctor

lessons.title: The thyroid thermostat

scenes.text: Pooja, 30, feels tired, cold, constipated and has gained weight.
Her TSH is high and free T4 low — hypothyroidism.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Feedback loop
steps.body: The hypothalamus releases **TRH** → pituitary releases **TSH** → thyroid makes **T4** (and some T3), which sets metabolism. High T4 suppresses TSH; low T4 raises TSH. So **high TSH usually means an underactive thyroid**, low TSH an overactive one.

steps.title: Iodine
steps.body: Thyroid hormones contain iodine. India's universal salt iodisation (National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme) greatly reduced goitre and iodine-deficiency disorders. In India, autoimmune **Hashimoto's thyroiditis** is a common cause of hypothyroidism.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking levothyroxine with tea, calcium or iron
- Stopping replacement when feeling better
- Ignoring a sore throat and fever on carbimazole
- Not telling the doctor about pregnancy early

activity.prompt: Match the lab pattern to the likely state.

lessons.title: Lab: Taking levothyroxine right

scenes.text: Pooja takes her thyroid tablet with tea and her calcium-iron supplement at breakfast.
Her TSH stays high. The problem is timing.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: **Levothyroxine** is synthetic T4, identical to the natural hormone. It replaces what the thyroid can't make. Usually lifelong in Hashimoto's.

steps.title: How it's commonly taken
steps.body: Once daily on an **empty stomach** (commonly 30–60 minutes before breakfast, with water), at the same time daily — or as your doctor advises. Keep the **same brand** if possible; switching may need a TSH check.

steps.title: Interactions
steps.body: Separate by several hours (commonly 4) from **calcium, iron, antacids**, and some others (e.g. sucralfate, cholestyramine). Soy, high-fibre and coffee can reduce absorption. PPIs may reduce it.

steps.title: Pregnancy
steps.body: Needs often **increase in pregnancy**; women on levothyroxine should inform their doctor as soon as pregnancy is confirmed for TSH checks and adjustment.

Breakfast and tea 30–60 minutes later
Calcium/iron supplement moved to evening (≥4 hours apart)
Same brand each refill when possible
TSH recheck about 6–8 weeks after any change

lessons.title: Lab: Overactive thyroid and the sore-throat rule

scenes.text: Imran, 28, has palpitations, weight loss, tremor and heat intolerance — Graves' disease.
He starts carbimazole and is given an important warning.

steps.title: Treatment options
steps.body: **Anti-thyroid drugs**: carbimazole/methimazole (block thyroid peroxidase → less hormone), propylthiouracil (PTU, used mainly in first-trimester pregnancy). **Beta blockers** relieve tremor and palpitations. Other options: **radioactive iodine**, surgery.

steps.title: Agranulocytosis
steps.body: Rarely, these drugs wipe out white cells (**agranulocytosis**). **Sore throat, mouth ulcers, fever** → stop and get an urgent blood count as instructed. PTU also carries a risk of serious liver injury. Carbimazole/methimazole in early pregnancy are linked to birth defects — planning matters.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking levothyroxine with tea, calcium or iron
- Stopping replacement when feeling better
- Ignoring a sore throat and fever on carbimazole
- Not telling the doctor about pregnancy early

choices.label: Contact the doctor urgently for a blood count, as warned
Take leftover antibiotics and continue

end1.text: Count was normal this time — a viral sore throat. Checking was still the right call.

end2.text: Agranulocytosis can cause overwhelming infection. Always follow the sore-throat rule.

lessons.title: What paracetamol is and how it works

scenes.text: Ananya, 24, has 101°F fever and a headache after a long train journey.
Her roommate offers a strip of paracetamol: 'It's the safest one, take as many as you want.'
Safe at the right amount — but 'as many as you want' is exactly how people end up in hospital. Let's understand why.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
**Paracetamol** (called **acetaminophen** in the USA and Japan) is an **analgesic** (pain reliever) and **antipyretic** (fever reducer). It is sold under many brand names, alone and inside combination cold, flu and pain products.

Unlike ibuprofen or aspirin it has **very little anti-inflammatory effect** — it will not reduce the swelling of a sprained ankle much.

steps.title: Mechanism in plain words
steps.body:
Fever happens when the brain's thermostat (the **hypothalamus**) is turned up by chemical messengers called **prostaglandins**. Paracetamol mainly reduces prostaglandin production **inside the brain and spinal cord**, so the thermostat is set back down and pain signals are dampened.

At pharmacology level: it is a weak inhibitor of the **cyclooxygenase (COX)** enzymes in peripheral tissues where peroxide levels are high (inflamed tissue), but works better centrally; other proposed pathways include a metabolite (AM404) acting on cannabinoid/TRPV1 systems and descending serotonergic pain pathways. The full mechanism is still debated.

steps.title: Why it is popular
steps.body:
- Gentle on the stomach compared with NSAIDs
- Does not thin the blood
- Generally preferred for fever in **dengue** (where NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and aspirin are avoided because of bleeding risk)
- Widely considered a first choice for pain and fever in pregnancy when a doctor agrees it is needed

steps.title: What fever medicine is really for
steps.body: Fever is a defence, not a disease. Paracetamol treats **discomfort**; it does not cure the infection. A fever that keeps coming back still needs its cause found.

statements.s: Paracetamol is a strong anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen.
statements.why: Its anti-inflammatory effect is weak; it mainly reduces pain and fever.

statements.s: Acetaminophen and paracetamol are the same medicine.
statements.why: Two names for one molecule in different countries.

statements.s: Paracetamol cures the infection that causes the fever.
Paracetamol does not thin the blood.
statements.why: Unlike aspirin, it has no meaningful antiplatelet effect.

options: Reducing prostaglandin production in the brain and spinal cord
quiz.why: Its main action is central prostaglandin reduction.

lessons.title: Lab: Why overdose damages the liver

scenes.text: Rahul took many tablets over a day for a toothache, plus a cold sachet that also contained paracetamol.
Next morning he feels only a bit nauseous and thinks he is fine.
Two days later he is jaundiced. Paracetamol poisoning often looks mild at first — that is what makes it dangerous.

steps.title: Normal metabolism
steps.body: At normal amounts the liver processes most paracetamol by **glucuronidation** and **sulfation** into harmless products excreted in urine. A small fraction goes through **CYP2E1** (and other cytochrome P450 enzymes) to a toxic, reactive molecule called **NAPQI**. The liver instantly neutralises NAPQI with its antioxidant **glutathione**.

steps.title: What happens in overdose
steps.body: With too much paracetamol the safe pathways get saturated, more goes to NAPQI, and **glutathione runs out**. NAPQI then binds to liver-cell proteins and kills the cells (**hepatocellular necrosis**). This can cause acute liver failure, which can be fatal or need a transplant.

steps.title: The typical timeline
steps.body:
- **First 24 h:** often no symptoms, or nausea, vomiting, sweating
- **24–72 h:** right upper abdominal pain, rising liver enzymes
- **72–96 h:** peak liver damage — jaundice, confusion, bleeding, low sugar
- Then recovery or liver failure

Feeling fine early does NOT mean safe.

steps.title: The antidote
steps.body: Hospitals give **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)**, which replenishes glutathione. It works best when started early (ideally within about 8 hours of ingestion) but is still given later. Doctors measure blood paracetamol levels and liver tests to decide.

steps.title: Who is at higher risk
steps.body:
- Regular heavy alcohol users
- People who are malnourished, fasting or have very low body weight
- Existing liver disease
- Some medicines that induce liver enzymes (e.g. some anti-epileptics, rifampicin) — check with a pharmacist

activity.prompt: Put the overdose chain of events in order.
items: Large amount of paracetamol is swallowed

More paracetamol is converted by CYP enzymes into NAPQI
Liver glutathione is used up
NAPQI binds liver-cell proteins and cells die
Liver enzymes rise and jaundice appears days later

lessons.title: Lab: Spot the hidden duplicate

scenes.text: Neha has a fever and a cold. On the counter: a 'fever tablet', a 'cold & flu' sachet and a 'headache' combo.
She reads the small print: all three contain paracetamol.
Taken together, she would be stacking doses without realising it.

steps.title: Read the composition, not the brand
steps.body: In India, the **composition** line (e.g. 'Each tablet contains: Paracetamol IP 500 mg') is printed on the strip or box. 'IP' means Indian Pharmacopoeia standard. Always compare compositions — brand names tell you nothing.

steps.title: Where paracetamol hides
steps.body:
- Cold and flu tablets/sachets (with phenylephrine, chlorphenamine, caffeine)
- 'Strong' headache tablets (with caffeine)
- Pain combos with ibuprofen, diclofenac, aceclofenac
- Some prescription painkillers combined with tramadol
- Children's syrups and drops (different strengths!)

steps.title: Label maximum
steps.body: Every pack states a **maximum in 24 hours** and a minimum gap between doses. Count every product you are taking toward that one maximum. For healthy adults, labels commonly state 4 g per 24 hours; many doctors advise less for people with risk factors. Children's amounts depend on weight — follow the label or doctor exactly.

steps.title: Ask the pharmacist one question
steps.body: 'Does anything else I'm taking already contain paracetamol?' — this single question prevents most accidental overdoses.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — handle a suspected paracetamol overdose

scenes.text: Your cousin, 19, texts: 'I took a whole strip after a fight with my parents. I feel ok though.'
This is both a poisoning emergency and possibly a mental-health crisis.
What you do in the next hour matters.

steps.title: Priorities
steps.body:
1. Safety: stay with them (in person or on the phone).
2. Call **112** or go to the nearest emergency department — do not wait for symptoms.
3. Take the packs/strips along; note the time taken and roughly how much.
4. Do not induce vomiting; do not give 'home remedies'.
5. Treat the emotional crisis with kindness: listen, don't lecture. Tele-MANAS **14416** offers mental-health support.

steps.title: What the hospital will do
steps.body: Blood paracetamol level (usually from 4 hours after ingestion), liver and kidney tests, clotting tests, and **N-acetylcysteine** if needed. Activated charcoal may be considered very early. A mental-health assessment is standard after intentional overdose.

steps.title: In India
steps.body: 112 connects police, fire and ambulance. Large hospitals have poison-information services. Intentional self-harm is treated as a medical and mental-health matter; seeking help is the right thing.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking two products that both contain paracetamol
- Thinking 'safe' means 'any amount is safe'
- Waiting for symptoms after an overdose instead of going to hospital
- Giving adult tablets or the wrong-strength syrup to children

lessons.title: COX, prostaglandins and how NSAIDs work

scenes.text: Kabir twists his knee in a weekend match. It is hot, swollen and painful.
Ibuprofen eases both the pain and the swelling — something paracetamol does less well.
Why? Because of an enzyme called cyclooxygenase.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Prostaglandins
steps.body: When tissue is injured, cell membranes release **arachidonic acid**. Enzymes called **cyclooxygenases (COX-1 and COX-2)** convert it into **prostaglandins** and **thromboxane**. Prostaglandins cause pain sensitisation, swelling, redness and fever.

steps.title: COX-1 vs COX-2
steps.body:
- **COX-1** is 'housekeeping': protects stomach lining (mucus, bicarbonate), supports kidney blood flow, helps platelets clump (thromboxane A2).
- **COX-2** is mostly switched on in inflammation.

**Ibuprofen** blocks both, reversibly. That is why it relieves inflammation (COX-2) but can damage the stomach and kidneys (COX-1).

steps.title: The NSAID family
steps.body: Ibuprofen, naproxen, diclofenac, aceclofenac, mefenamic acid, ketorolac, aspirin (special case), and the COX-2 selective 'coxibs' (e.g. celecoxib, etoricoxib) which are gentler on the stomach but carry cardiovascular cautions.

steps.title: Used for
steps.body: Pain with inflammation (sprains, dental pain, period pain, arthritis flares), fever, headaches. Take with food reduces stomach upset but does not remove bleeding risk.

activity.prompt: Match the term to its role.
pairs: Raw material released from cell membranes

lessons.title: Lab: Who must be careful with NSAIDs

scenes.text: Pharmacist Farah gets five customers in an hour all asking for 'a strong painkiller'.
Some can take an NSAID; some really should not without a doctor.
You sort them like she does.

steps.title: Stomach and gut
steps.body: NSAIDs can cause gastritis, ulcers and **GI bleeding**, sometimes without warning pain. Risk rises with age over ~65, previous ulcer, high or long use, alcohol, and use with steroids, blood thinners or SSRIs.

steps.title: Kidneys
steps.body: Prostaglandins keep kidney blood flow up when you are **dehydrated**. NSAIDs during vomiting/diarrhoea, heatstroke, or with BP drugs (ACE inhibitors/ARBs) plus diuretics ('triple whammy') can cause **acute kidney injury**.

steps.title: Heart and blood pressure
steps.body: NSAIDs (including coxibs and diclofenac) can raise BP, cause fluid retention and modestly increase heart attack and stroke risk, especially with long use or in people with heart disease.

steps.title: Asthma and pregnancy
steps.body: A minority of people with asthma (especially with nasal polyps) have **NSAID-exacerbated respiratory disease**. In pregnancy, NSAIDs are generally avoided, particularly from about 20 weeks and in the third trimester, unless a doctor advises.

lessons.title: Lab: Recognise a GI bleed and other red flags

scenes.text: Rajan uncle, 70, has taken painkillers daily for knee pain for weeks, bought without a prescription.
He feels dizzy and his stools have turned black and sticky.
That is a classic sign of bleeding in the upper gut.

steps.title: Red flags — seek urgent care (112)
steps.body:
- Black, tarry stools (melaena) or vomiting blood / 'coffee-ground' material
- Fainting, fast pulse, pale and sweaty
- Severe abdominal pain
- Sudden swelling, very little urine
- Wheeze or face swelling after a dose

steps.title: Iron and black stools
steps.body: Iron tablets and bismuth can also darken stools — but if someone on NSAIDs has black stools with dizziness, treat it as a bleed until a doctor says otherwise.

steps.title: Reducing risk (with a doctor)
steps.body: Lowest effective amount for shortest time; avoid combining two NSAIDs; doctors may add a stomach protector (PPI) for high-risk people; review long-term use regularly.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking NSAIDs on an empty stomach for weeks without review
- Using them during dengue or severe dehydration
- Combining two NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen + diclofenac)
- Ignoring black stools or dizziness

lessons.title: Willow bark to wonder drug: how aspirin works

scenes.text: Dadaji takes a small 'heart tablet' every day after his angioplasty.
It is aspirin — the same molecule people once took in larger amounts for headaches.
At low dose it does something special to platelets.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: History
steps.body: Willow bark (containing salicin) was used for pain for millennia. **Acetylsalicylic acid** was produced as a stable medicine by Bayer chemists in 1897 and marketed as Aspirin in 1899. Its mechanism (prostaglandin inhibition) was described by John Vane, who shared the 1982 Nobel Prize.

steps.title: Irreversible blocker
steps.body: Aspirin **acetylates** a serine in the COX enzyme, permanently switching it off. Most cells make new COX, but **platelets have no nucleus** and cannot. So one dose blocks a platelet's thromboxane A2 for its whole lifespan of about **7–10 days**. That is why the antiplatelet effect lasts long after the drug is gone.

steps.title: Uses
steps.body:
- **Low dose:** prevention of further heart attacks/strokes in people who already have cardiovascular disease (secondary prevention), after stents — on a doctor's advice
- **Higher doses:** pain, fever, inflammation (now less used; other options safer)

For people **without** heart disease, routine daily aspirin is no longer generally recommended because bleeding risk can outweigh benefit — decide with a doctor.

steps.title: Before procedures
steps.body: Tell your dentist or surgeon you take aspirin. Never stop prescribed aspirin after a stent on your own — this can cause stent clotting. The doctor decides.

cards.front: Why does one dose affect platelets for days?
cards.back: Platelets have no nucleus, cannot make new COX; lifespan ~7–10 days

options: Is no longer generally recommended; decide with a doctor

lessons.title: Children, viral illness and Reye syndrome

scenes.text: Little Isha, 8, has chickenpox and fever.
A neighbour hands her mother an aspirin: 'This always worked for my kids.'
Her mother remembers: aspirin is not for children with viral illness.

steps.title: Reye syndrome
steps.body: **Reye syndrome** is a rare but serious condition causing **brain swelling and liver damage**, linked to aspirin use in children and teenagers recovering from viral infections, especially **influenza and chickenpox**. After warnings against aspirin in children, cases fell dramatically.

steps.title: The rule
steps.body: Many regulators advise **no aspirin for children and teenagers** (UK: under 16) unless a specialist prescribes it for a specific condition (e.g. Kawasaki disease). Check hidden aspirin/salicylates in some combination products and gels.

steps.title: Signs
steps.body: Persistent vomiting, confusion, unusual sleepiness, aggression or seizures a few days after a viral illness → emergency care (112).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving aspirin to children or teenagers with viral illness
- Starting daily aspirin without a doctor
- Stopping prescribed aspirin after a stent on your own
- Forgetting to tell the dentist or surgeon

lessons.title: Lab: Salicylate poisoning — recognise it

scenes.text: A woman with arthritis has been taking extra aspirin for weeks.
Now her ears ring, she is breathing fast and feels confused.
These are classic salicylate toxicity signs.

steps.title: What happens
steps.body: High salicylate levels: stimulate the breathing centre (fast deep breathing → **respiratory alkalosis**), then disturb cell energy production (uncoupling oxidative phosphorylation → heat, **metabolic acidosis**). Effects: **tinnitus** (ringing ears), deafness, nausea, vomiting, sweating, fever, confusion, seizures, and potentially death.

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: Any suspected aspirin overdose → **112** / emergency department. Chronic toxicity in older people is often missed because it looks like infection or confusion. Hospital treatment may include activated charcoal, IV fluids, urine alkalinisation with bicarbonate, and dialysis in severe cases.

steps.title: Hidden salicylates
steps.body: Oil of wintergreen (methyl salicylate) in some balms and liniments is highly toxic if swallowed — even a small amount can be dangerous to a child. Store pain balms out of reach.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Giving aspirin to children or teenagers with viral illness

- Stopping prescribed aspirin after a stent on your own
- Forgetting to tell the dentist or surgeon

lessons.title: Diclofenac: strength and caution

scenes.text: Sameer, 38, has back pain from long hours at a laptop.
He has been taking a diclofenac combo 'whenever needed' for months.
His BP at a health check is higher than last year.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: **Diclofenac** is an NSAID with relatively stronger COX-2 than COX-1 effect. It treats musculoskeletal pain, arthritis, migraine attacks, dental and post-operative pain. **Aceclofenac** is a related drug that is converted partly into diclofenac in the body.

steps.title: Heart caution
steps.body: European and UK regulators (2013) concluded that systemic diclofenac carries a cardiovascular risk similar to COX-2 inhibitors and advised against it in people with established heart disease, peripheral artery disease or stroke. It can also raise BP and harm kidneys and the liver (liver enzyme rises).

steps.title: Treat the cause
steps.body: For chronic desk back pain, posture, movement breaks, strengthening and physiotherapy usually do more long-term good than repeated tablets.

statements.s: Diclofenac is safe in people with heart disease.
statements.why: Regulators advise against systemic use there.

statements.s: Aceclofenac is related to diclofenac.
Long-term NSAID use can raise blood pressure.
Painkillers fix the cause of posture back pain.

lessons.title: Lab: Tablet, gel or injection?

scenes.text: At a local clinic, a patient asks for a painkiller injection because 'it works faster and is stronger'.
Is that true? And is it safe?

steps.title: Topical gels
steps.body: Topical NSAIDs (e.g. diclofenac gel) put drug near superficial joints/muscles with much lower blood levels, so fewer stomach and kidney effects. Useful for knee and hand osteoarthritis and sprains. Don't apply on broken skin, avoid eyes, wash hands, and avoid sunlight on treated skin for some products.

steps.title: Injections
steps.body: Injected painkillers are **not safer** — they carry the same systemic side effects, plus injection risks: **sciatic nerve injury**, abscess, tissue damage, and rare severe allergic reactions (anaphylaxis). Unsterile injections spread hepatitis B/C and HIV. Injections should be used only when a clinician has a good reason (e.g. cannot swallow).

steps.title: Speed
steps.body: Oral NSAIDs typically start working within about 30–60 minutes. For most outpatient pain, oral or topical routes are enough.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing injections are stronger and safer
- Long-term tablets for desk back pain instead of fixing the cause
- Applying gel to broken skin
- Giving human painkillers to animals without a vet

lessons.title: The vulture collapse — medicines in the environment

scenes.text: In the 1980s, India had tens of millions of vultures cleaning carcasses.
By the mid-2000s, populations of some species had fallen by more than 95%.
The cause: diclofenac given to cattle, left in carcasses the vultures ate.

steps.title: What happened
steps.body: Vultures feeding on carcasses of cattle recently treated with diclofenac developed **kidney failure** and **visceral gout**. Gyps vultures (white-rumped, Indian, slender-billed) declined catastrophically.

steps.title: Response
steps.body: India banned **veterinary diclofenac in 2006**; later restricted large human multi-dose vials to curb misuse in animals. **Meloxicam** was found safe for vultures and promoted as an alternative. Breeding centres and 'vulture safe zones' followed. Other veterinary NSAIDs (e.g. ketoprofen, aceclofenac) are also harmful and some have since been banned for veterinary use.

steps.title: Why it matters to people
steps.body: Fewer vultures meant more rotting carcasses, more feral dogs and a rise in rabies risk — a lesson in how a medicine can harm whole ecosystems. Never give human medicines to animals without a vet.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Believing injections are stronger and safer
- Long-term tablets for desk back pain instead of fixing the cause
- Applying gel to broken skin
- Giving human painkillers to animals without a vet

steps.title: When to see a professional

lessons.title: What's inside the sachet

scenes.text: Priya has a blocked nose, sneezing and mild fever during the monsoon.
Her cold tablet lists four ingredients.
Each does a different job — and each has its own side effects.

steps.title: Learning, not medical advice
steps.body: This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Typical ingredients
steps.body:
- **Paracetamol:** fever, aches
- **Phenylephrine** (or other decongestants): narrows blood vessels in the nose → less stuffiness; can raise BP and heart rate
- **Chlorphenamine** (first-generation antihistamine): reduces sneezing/runny nose; causes **drowsiness** and dry mouth
- **Caffeine:** counters drowsiness, mild pain boost; can cause palpitations and poor sleep
- Cough products may add **dextromethorphan** (suppressant), **guaifenesin**/ambroxol (mucus), or codeine (prescription, restricted)

steps.title: Evidence note
steps.body: In 2023 a US FDA advisory committee concluded that **oral phenylephrine** at standard doses is not effective as a nasal decongestant. Nasal sprays and some other decongestants work, but have their own cautions.

steps.title: Colds are viral
steps.body: Most colds settle in 7–10 days. Combos only ease symptoms. Rest, fluids, steam/saline rinses help too. Antibiotics do not cure a cold.

lessons.title: Lab: Who should avoid which ingredient

scenes.text: The whole Sharma family has a cold. One box of combo tablets.
Not everyone should take it.

steps.title: Decongestant cautions
steps.body: High BP, heart disease, overactive thyroid, glaucoma (angle-closure), enlarged prostate, and people on **MAO inhibitors** should check with a doctor first.

steps.title: Drowsy antihistamine cautions
steps.body: Not before driving or operating machinery; worse with **alcohol** and other sedatives; elderly at risk of confusion and falls; can worsen urinary retention and glaucoma.

steps.title: Children
steps.body: Cough-cold combination products are not recommended for **young children** without a doctor — they have caused serious harm and offer little proven benefit. In India, regulators have required warnings against certain combinations (such as chlorphenamine with phenylephrine) for children under 4. Contaminated cough syrups (diethylene glycol) have also caused child deaths globally — buy only from licensed pharmacies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Taking a cold combo plus a separate paracetamol tablet
- Driving after a drowsy antihistamine
- Giving combos to young children without a doctor
- Expecting antibiotics to cure a cold

lessons.title: Lab: Read a combo label like a pharmacist

scenes.text: Box A: Paracetamol 500 mg, Phenylephrine 10 mg, Chlorphenamine 2 mg. Box B: Paracetamol 650 mg.
A customer wants to take both for a 'bad cold'.

steps.title: Label checklist
steps.body:
1. Composition (generic names + strengths)
2. Directions and maximum per 24 h
3. Warnings (drowsiness, BP, children)
4. Batch number, manufacturing and expiry dates
5. Storage
6. Schedule markings (e.g. Rx-only)

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: One Box A tablet + one Box B tablet = 500 + 650 = **1,150 mg paracetamol** in one go. Repeating that every few hours quickly approaches or passes the label maximum. Choose one product only.

scenes.text: Half the hostel floor has flu-like illness.

steps.title: See a doctor if
steps.body:
- Fever lasting more than 3 days, or very high fever
- Breathlessness, chest pain, bluish lips
- Confusion, stiff neck, rash that doesn't fade
- Severe dehydration
- Infants, pregnancy, elderly, chronic illness
- In dengue/malaria-prone seasons, fever needs testing

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Hand washing, covering coughs, ventilation, staying home when sick, annual flu vaccine for high-risk groups.

- Expecting antibiotics to cure a cold
